implementation_notes: The BCL mechanism: derive from DispatchProxy, implement Invoke(MethodInfo, object?[]), and let DispatchProxy.Create<T, TProxy>() emit a proxy type that implements the interface and routes every member to that one method. It is interface-based, so the proxy is typed as the interface and the target's fields are unreachable through it; the generated type is cached per (proxy type, interface) pair. Use it when the interface set is known only at runtime; when it is known at compile time a hand-written decorator stays clearer.
pitfalls: DispatchProxy emits IL at runtime, so trimming and NativeAOT report it as RequiresDynamicCode - the same design silently stops working when the deployment target changes.
Only interfaces can be proxied: members the interface does not carry are invisible on the proxy, and method.Invoke wraps target exceptions instead of letting them through.
Async methods return Task, so an interceptor that does not await them swallows the exception that would have been observed by the caller.

variants.name: Castle.Core DynamicProxy with an interceptor pipeline
variants.implementation_notes: Castle.Core's DynamicProxy is the dominant third-party realization: ProxyGenerator emits the proxy type, an IInterceptor chain receives Invocation objects, and two models exist - composition (CreateInterfaceProxyWithTarget, like DispatchProxy) and inheritance (CreateClassProxy, where the proxy derives from the target so internal calls are intercepted too). Choose it when virtual members of a class must be proxied or when interceptor composition is needed; the price is a third-party dependency and the rule that only virtual, non-final members can be overridden.
pitfalls: A new ProxyGenerator per call bypasses the type cache and leaks dynamic assemblies; the generator must be a long-lived single instance.
Inheritance proxying only works for virtual, non-final methods on non-sealed classes, and constructor bypass tricks (Objenesis) can skip field initialisation.
Composition proxies do not intercept calls the target makes on itself, so behaviour added this way misses internal calls.

variants.name: build-time generated forwarding type
variants.idiom_name: incremental source generator emitting one forwarding member per interface method
variants.implementation_notes: An IIncrementalGenerator (Roslyn) can emit the forwarding type at compile time from the same interface declaration, so no IL is generated at runtime and the result survives trimming, NativeAOT and source-link audits. The cost is a build step and one generated proxy per interface that opts in, plus regenerated code whenever the interface changes - the standard .NET answer when runtime code generation is not allowed.
pitfalls: Generated code drifts when the interface changes but the generator is not re-run in the editor or in CI; the build then fails in generated code the developer never wrote.
The generated proxy is a compile-time artifact: members the interface gains later only appear after regeneration, so a deployment can carry a stale forwarding surface.
